title: Rectangle Overlap
notes:
Task and constraints: Rectangle Overlap requires checking its defining condition on the supplied input and returning the specified boolean, count, index, or transformed structure.
Idea: `isRectangleOverlap` checks strict overlap on both x projections and both y projections using the rectangles' left, bottom, right, and top coordinates.
Technique and why it applies: The four inequalities require positive intersection width and height, excluding boundary-only contact.
Invariant: Positive-area overlap requires intersection length greater than zero on both axes.
Edge cases: Touching edges or corners do not overlap because every comparison is strict.
Complexity: O(1) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: The four inequalities require positive intersection width and height, excluding boundary-only contact.

title: Rectangle Overlap
notes:
Task and constraints: Rectangle Overlap requires checking its defining condition on the supplied input and returning the specified boolean, count, index, or transformed structure.
Idea: `isRectangleOverlap` returns the conjunction of four strict coordinate comparisons between rectangles `a` and `b`.
Technique and why it applies: A constant number of interval comparisons determines overlap without constructing a rectangle.
Invariant: Both horizontal intervals and both vertical intervals must intersect with positive length.
Edge cases: Equal edges mean no positive-area overlap; coordinates use the standard `[left,bottom,right,top]` layout.
Complexity: O(1) time and O(1) space.
code: class Solution { public boolean isRectangleOverlap(int[] a,int[] b){return a[0]<b[2]&&b[0]<a[2]&&a[1]<b[3]&&b[1]<a[3];} }
complexity_reason: A constant number of interval comparisons determines overlap without constructing a rectangle.

title: Magic Squares In Grid
notes:
Task and constraints: Magic Squares In Grid requires checking its defining condition on the supplied input and returning the specified boolean, count, index, or transformed structure.
Idea: `numMagicSquaresInside` checks every 3x3 window for the digits 1 through 9 exactly once, center 5, and eight line sums of 15.
Technique and why it applies: The nine-cell uniqueness and line-sum tests completely validate each possible 3x3 candidate.
Invariant: A window is counted only after its uniqueness, range, center, row, column, and diagonal tests all pass.
Edge cases: Windows require at least three rows and columns; the fixed-size checks assume a non-empty rectangular grid.
Complexity: O(mn) time and O(1) auxiliary space per fixed-size window.
complexity_reason: The nine-cell uniqueness and line-sum tests completely validate each possible 3x3 candidate.

title: Magic Squares In Grid
notes:
Task and constraints: Magic Squares In Grid requires checking its defining condition on the supplied input and returning the specified boolean, count, index, or transformed structure.
Idea: `numMagicSquaresInside` marks seen values 1 through 9, requires center 5, then verifies each row, column, and both diagonals sum to 15.
Technique and why it applies: The fixed boolean array checks uniqueness while explicit row, column, and diagonal sums verify magic totals.
Invariant: The boolean `ok` remains true only when all digits are valid and every magic-square condition holds.
Edge cases: A grid smaller than 3x3 has no candidates; out-of-range or duplicate values reject the window.
Complexity: O(mn) time and O(1) auxiliary space because each candidate has fixed dimensions.
code: class Solution { public int numMagicSquaresInside(int[][]g){int m=g.length,n=g[0].length,ans=0;for(int r=0;r+2<m;r++)for(int c=0;c+2<n;c++){boolean[]seen=new boolean[10];boolean ok=true;for(int i=r;i<r+3;i++)for(int k=c;k<c+3;k++){int v=g[i][k];if(v<1||v>9||seen[v])ok=false;else seen[v]=true;}if(!ok||g[r+1][c+1]!=5)continue;for(int i=0;i<3;i++){int row=0,col=0;for(int k=0;k<3;k++){row+=g[r+i][c+k];col+=g[r+k][c+i];}if(row!=15||col!=15)ok=false;}if(g[r][c]+g[r+1][c+1]+g[r+2][c+2]!=15||g[r][c+2]+g[r+1][c+1]+g[r+2][c]!=15)ok=false;if(ok)ans++;}return ans;} }
complexity_reason: The fixed boolean array checks uniqueness while explicit row, column, and diagonal sums verify magic totals.

title: Backspace String Compare
notes:
Task and constraints: Backspace String Compare requires checking its defining condition on the supplied input and returning the specified boolean, count, index, or transformed structure.
Idea: `backspaceCompare` uses `build` to push normal characters and pop one character for `#`, then compares the two built strings.
Technique and why it applies: Stack-like character lists implement backspace semantics directly before equality comparison.
Invariant: After each input character, `out` is the effective text after all backspaces in the processed prefix.
Edge cases: A backspace on an empty result does nothing; the two strings may have different raw lengths.
Complexity: O(n+m) time and O(n+m) auxiliary space for both results.
complexity_reason: Stack-like character lists implement backspace semantics directly before equality comparison.

title: Backspace String Compare
notes:
Task and constraints: Backspace String Compare requires checking its defining condition on the supplied input and returning the specified boolean, count, index, or transformed structure.
Idea: `backspaceCompare` compares strings returned by `build`, which appends ordinary characters and deletes the last builder character for `#` when available.
Technique and why it applies: Deleting the last builder character reproduces the backspace operation while safely ignoring empty-stack deletes.
Invariant: The builder contains exactly the visible characters after processing each prefix.
Edge cases: Leading or repeated backspaces leave an empty builder unchanged; raw string lengths need not match.
Complexity: O(n+m) time and O(n+m) space for the constructed strings.
code: class Solution { public boolean backspaceCompare(String s,String t){return build(s).equals(build(t));}private String build(String x){StringBuilder b=new StringBuilder();for(char c:x.toCharArray()){if(c=='#'){if(b.length()>0)b.deleteCharAt(b.length()-1);}else b.append(c);}return b.toString();} }
complexity_reason: Deleting the last builder character reproduces the backspace operation while safely ignoring empty-stack deletes.

title: Maximize Distance to Closest Person
notes:
Task and constraints: Maximize Distance to Closest Person requires checking its defining condition on the supplied input and returning the specified boolean, count, index, or transformed structure.
Idea: `maxDistToClosest` tracks the previous occupied seat and updates the best distance using the leading gap or half of each interior gap, then checks the trailing gap.
Technique and why it applies: Interior gaps favor their midpoint, while edge gaps favor the empty seat farthest from the only nearby person.
Invariant: `prev` identifies the last occupied index, and `best` is the largest candidate distance seen so far.
Edge cases: Leading and trailing empty runs have no occupied seat on one side, so their full lengths are candidates.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Interior gaps favor their midpoint, while edge gaps favor the empty seat farthest from the only nearby person.

title: Maximize Distance to Closest Person
notes:
Task and constraints: Maximize Distance to Closest Person requires checking its defining condition on the supplied input and returning the specified boolean, count, index, or transformed structure.
Idea: `maxDistToClosest` scans occupied indices, considers `i` for the leading gap and `(i-prev)/2` for interior gaps, then checks the suffix after the last person.
Technique and why it applies: The midpoint of an interior gap maximizes the minimum distance to its two occupied endpoints.
Invariant: `best` is the maximum nearest-person distance among all completed gaps.
Edge cases: The first occupied seat uses `prev=-1`; the final expression handles trailing empty seats.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code: class Solution { public int maxDistToClosest(int[] seats){int n=seats.length,prev=-1,best=0;for(int i=0;i<n;i++)if(seats[i]==1){best=Math.max(best,prev==-1?i:(i-prev)/2);prev=i;}return Math.max(best,n-1-prev);} }
complexity_reason: The midpoint of an interior gap maximizes the minimum distance to its two occupied endpoints.

title: Peak Index in a Mountain Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Peak Index in a Mountain Array requires checking its defining condition on the supplied input and returning the specified boolean, count, index, or transformed structure.
Idea: `peakIndexInMountainArray` binary-searches while `lo < hi`, moving right when `arr[mid] < arr[mid+1]` and otherwise moving `hi` to `mid`.
Technique and why it applies: An increasing slope means the peak lies to the right; a falling slope keeps the peak at or left of midpoint.
Invariant: The peak remains inside the inclusive interval `[lo,hi]` after every comparison.
Edge cases: The input is guaranteed to strictly rise and then strictly fall, so a peak exists and has a successor when `mid` is checked.
Complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: An increasing slope means the peak lies to the right; a falling slope keeps the peak at or left of midpoint.

title: Peak Index in a Mountain Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Peak Index in a Mountain Array requires checking its defining condition on the supplied input and returning the specified boolean, count, index, or transformed structure.
Idea: `peakIndexInMountainArray` compares `arr[mid]` with `arr[mid+1]` and shrinks the binary-search interval toward the peak.
Technique and why it applies: The slope comparison identifies which side still contains the unique mountain peak.
Invariant: The mountain peak always lies within the updated `lo` and `hi` bounds.
Edge cases: Strict mountain constraints ensure `mid+1` is valid while `lo < hi` and there is one peak.
Complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code: class Solution { public int peakIndexInMountainArray(int[] arr){int lo=0,hi=arr.length-1;while(lo<hi){int mid=lo+(hi-lo)/2;if(arr[mid]<arr[mid+1])lo=mid+1;else hi=mid;}return lo;} }
complexity_reason: The slope comparison identifies which side still contains the unique mountain peak.

title: Buddy Strings
approach_name: Check duplicates or two swapped positions
notes:
Task and constraints: Buddy Strings requires checking its defining condition on the supplied input and returning the specified boolean, count, index, or transformed structure.
Idea: `buddyStrings` rejects unequal lengths, handles identical strings by checking for duplicate characters, and otherwise verifies exactly two mismatches that cross-match.
Technique and why it applies: Exactly two cross-matching mismatch positions characterize a successful swap when the strings differ.
Invariant: For different strings, the mismatch list must contain exactly two positions whose characters swap into the goal.
Edge cases: Identical strings need a repeated character to allow a swap; three or more mismatches cannot be repaired by one swap.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space for the mismatch list and set.
complexity_reason: Exactly two cross-matching mismatch positions characterize a successful swap when the strings differ.

title: Buddy Strings
approach_name: Check duplicates or two swapped positions
notes:
Task and constraints: Buddy Strings requires checking its defining condition on the supplied input and returning the specified boolean, count, index, or transformed structure.
Idea: `buddyStrings` handles equal strings with a duplicate-character scan, otherwise records at most two mismatch indices and checks their characters cross-match.
Technique and why it applies: The two mismatch indices must cross-match, while the equal-string case needs a duplicate to swap.
Invariant: A successful unequal pair has exactly two mismatch positions that exchange values.
Edge cases: Equal strings need a repeated letter; a third mismatch returns false immediately.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space for the fixed-size seen array and mismatch indices.
code: class Solution { public boolean buddyStrings(String s,String goal){if(s.length()!=goal.length())return false;if(s.equals(goal)){boolean[]seen=new boolean[26];for(char c:s.toCharArray()){if(seen[c-'a'])return true;seen[c-'a']=true;}return false;}int a=-1,b=-1;for(int i=0;i<s.length();i++)if(s.charAt(i)!=goal.charAt(i)){if(a<0)a=i;else if(b<0)b=i;else return false;}return b>=0&&s.charAt(a)==goal.charAt(b)&&s.charAt(b)==goal.charAt(a);} }
complexity_reason: The two mismatch indices must cross-match, while the equal-string case needs a duplicate to swap.

title: Lemonade Change
approach_name: Prefer giving a ten and five
notes:
Task and constraints: Lemonade Change requires checking its defining condition on the supplied input and returning the specified boolean, count, index, or transformed structure.
Idea: `lemonadeChange` tracks counts of fives and tens, gives a five for a ten-dollar bill, and prefers one ten plus one five for a twenty-dollar bill.
Technique and why it applies: Using a ten and five for a twenty preserves more fives for future ten-dollar customers.
Invariant: The counters represent available bills after serving all customers processed so far.
Edge cases: A ten requires one five; a twenty uses ten-plus-five when possible, otherwise three fives; impossible change returns false.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: Using a ten and five for a twenty preserves more fives for future ten-dollar customers.

title: Lemonade Change
approach_name: Prefer giving a ten and five
notes:
Task and constraints: Lemonade Change requires checking its defining condition on the supplied input and returning the specified boolean, count, index, or transformed structure.
Idea: `lemonadeChange` updates `five` and `ten` for each bill and uses a ten-plus-five combination before falling back to three fives for a twenty.
Technique and why it applies: The greedy preference for ten-plus-five preserves scarce five-dollar bills for later customers.
Invariant: The bill counters represent exactly the change inventory remaining after each successful transaction.
Edge cases: If no required change combination exists, the method returns false immediately.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code: class Solution { public boolean lemonadeChange(int[] bills){int five=0,ten=0;for(int b:bills){if(b==5)five++;else if(b==10){if(five==0)return false;five--;ten++;}else{if(ten>0&&five>0){ten--;five--;}else if(five>=3)five-=3;else return false;}}return true;} }
complexity_reason: The greedy preference for ten-plus-five preserves scarce five-dollar bills for later customers.

title: Transpose Matrix
notes:
Task and constraints: Transpose Matrix requires checking its defining condition on the supplied input and returning the specified boolean, count, index, or transformed structure.
Idea: `transpose` constructs each output row by fixing an original column `c` and collecting `matrix[r][c]` across all original rows.
Technique and why it applies: Swapping row and column indices turns each original column into one output row.
Invariant: Output coordinate `(c,r)` receives the input value from `(r,c)`.
Edge cases: A rectangular matrix swaps dimensions; the implementation assumes at least one input row.
Complexity: O(mn) time and O(mn) output space.
code:
class Solution:
 def transpose(self,matrix):return [[matrix[r][c] for r in range(len(matrix))] for c in range(len(matrix[0]))]
complexity_reason: Swapping row and column indices turns each original column into one output row.

title: Transpose Matrix
notes:
Task and constraints: Transpose Matrix requires checking its defining condition on the supplied input and returning the specified boolean, count, index, or transformed structure.
Idea: `transpose` allocates an `n`-by-`m` output and writes `out[c][r] = matrix[r][c]` for every input cell.
Technique and why it applies: The assignment reverses coordinate order while visiting each original matrix cell exactly once.
Invariant: Each original cell is copied to the position with row and column indices exchanged.
Edge cases: Rectangular dimensions are reversed; the implementation assumes a non-empty matrix.
Complexity: O(mn) time and O(mn) output space.
code: class Solution { public int[][] transpose(int[][] matrix){int[][]out=new int[matrix[0].length][matrix.length];for(int r=0;r<matrix.length;r++)for(int c=0;c<matrix[0].length;c++)out[c][r]=matrix[r][c];return out;} }
complexity_reason: The assignment reverses coordinate order while visiting each original matrix cell exactly once.

title: Binary Gap
notes:
Task and constraints: Binary Gap requires checking its defining condition on the supplied input and returning the specified boolean, count, index, or transformed structure.
Idea: `binaryGap` shifts `n` right one bit at a time, records positions where `n&1` is set, and updates the gap from the previous set-bit position.
Technique and why it applies: Only distances between consecutive set bits matter, so recording the last position is sufficient.
Invariant: `last` is the most recent set-bit position, and `best` is the largest consecutive-set-bit distance.
Edge cases: A number with fewer than two set bits has no gap and returns zero.
Complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: Only distances between consecutive set bits matter, so recording the last position is sufficient.

title: Binary Gap
notes:
Task and constraints: Binary Gap requires checking its defining condition on the supplied input and returning the specified boolean, count, index, or transformed structure.
Idea: `binaryGap` checks the low bit, updates `best` against `pos-last`, then shifts the integer and increments `pos`.
Technique and why it applies: Bitwise shifting visits every binary position and avoids allocating a binary string.
Invariant: `last` tracks the preceding one-bit position; `best` stores the maximum gap among processed ones.
Edge cases: Numbers with fewer than two set bits leave `best` at zero.
Complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code: class Solution { public int binaryGap(int n){int last=-1,best=0,pos=0;while(n>0){if((n&1)==1){if(last>=0)best=Math.max(best,pos-last);last=pos;}pos++;n>>=1;}return best;} }
complexity_reason: Bitwise shifting visits every binary position and avoids allocating a binary string.

title: Leaf-Similar Trees
notes:
Task and constraints: Leaf-Similar Trees requires checking its defining condition on the supplied input and returning the specified boolean, count, index, or transformed structure.
Idea: `leafSimilar` builds each tree's leaf list with an explicit stack, pushing right before left so leaves are collected left-to-right, then compares the lists.
Technique and why it applies: Pushing right before left makes the LIFO traversal visit left subtrees first.
Invariant: Each list contains leaf values in left-to-right traversal order.
Edge cases: Null roots produce empty lists; right-first stack pushes preserve left-first visit order.
Complexity: O(n+m) time and O(n+m) space for both leaf sequences and stacks.
complexity_reason: Pushing right before left makes the LIFO traversal visit left subtrees first.

title: Leaf-Similar Trees
notes:
Task and constraints: Leaf-Similar Trees requires checking its defining condition on the supplied input and returning the specified boolean, count, index, or transformed structure.
Idea: `leafSimilar` compares `leaves(a)` and `leaves(b)`; `leaves` uses an `ArrayDeque` and pushes right children before left children.
Technique and why it applies: The stack order preserves left-to-right leaf sequence, making list equality the required comparison.
Invariant: The list contains leaf values in the same left-to-right order used by the definition.
Edge cases: Null roots return empty lists; a node is a leaf only when both children are null.
Complexity: O(n+m) time and O(n+m) space for traversal and leaf lists.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public boolean leafSimilar(TreeNode a,TreeNode b){return leaves(a).equals(leaves(b));}private List<Integer> leaves(TreeNode root){List<Integer>out=new ArrayList<>();if(root==null)return out;ArrayDeque<TreeNode>st=new ArrayDeque<>();st.push(root);while(!st.isEmpty()){TreeNode n=st.pop();if(n.left==null&&n.right==null)out.add(n.val);else{if(n.right!=null)st.push(n.right);if(n.left!=null)st.push(n.left);}}return out;} }
complexity_reason: The stack order preserves left-to-right leaf sequence, making list equality the required comparison.
